subject: biology-hl
about: Original practice questions written for NevaIB from the IB guide's syllabus understandings and the school's unit order. Not IB past-paper questions, not publisher material and not IB markschemes: the marking points are written for self-marking. Organisms, experiments and data in data-response items are invented for practice.

items.stem: During transcription, which enzyme links RNA nucleotides together?
choices: DNA polymerase
Helicase
RNA polymerase
Ligase
items.note: RNA polymerase separates the DNA strands and joins RNA nucleotides complementary to the template strand. DNA polymerase is for replication.

items.stem: Which base in RNA pairs with adenine on the DNA template strand?
choices: Thymine
Guanine
Cytosine
Uracil
items.note: RNA has uracil instead of thymine, so A on the template pairs with U in mRNA.

choices: Three bases on mRNA that code for one amino acid
Three bases on a tRNA molecule that pair with mRNA
One base on mRNA that codes for one amino acid
Three amino acids joined by peptide bonds
items.note: Codons are mRNA triplets; anticodons are the complementary triplets on tRNA.

items.stem: The genetic code is described as degenerate because:
choices: Each codon can code for more than one different amino acid
More than one codon can code for the same amino acid
The code is different in different organisms
Some codons have only two bases
items.note: 64 codons for 20 amino acids — e.g. several codons for leucine. It is also (almost) universal.

items.stem: A DNA template strand reads 3′–TAC GGA TTC–5′. What is the mRNA sequence?
choices: 5′–ATG CCT AAG–3′
5′–AUG CCU AAG–3′
5′–UAC GGA UUC–3′
5′–AUG CCU AAC–3′
items.note: Pair each base (A–U, T–A, C–G, G–C) and write mRNA 5′→3′, antiparallel to the template.

items.stem: During translation, the role of tRNA is to:
choices: Carry the code from the nucleus to the ribosome
Join amino acids together with peptide bonds as a catalyst
Copy the base sequence of the DNA template strand into RNA
Carry a specific amino acid and pair its anticodon with a codon
items.note: Each tRNA has an anticodon and carries the matching amino acid. The ribosome (rRNA) catalyses peptide bonds.

items.stem: A substitution changes one base so that GAA becomes GAG; both code for glutamic acid. The effect on the protein is:
choices: None, because the amino acid sequence is unchanged
One amino acid is replaced, changing the shape
The protein is shortened by a stop codon
Every amino acid after the mutation changes
items.note: A silent mutation, possible because the code is degenerate.

choices: The start codon AUG at the beginning of the gene
The first exon after the terminator sequence
A promoter, a non-coding sequence upstream of the gene
Any point where the DNA strands happen to separate
items.note: The promoter is where RNA polymerase (with transcription factors) binds. AUG is a translation start, on mRNA.

choices: One gene to code for several different polypeptides
One mRNA to be translated by several ribosomes at once
Introns to be translated into short peptides
Exons to be removed so the mRNA is shorter
items.note: Different combinations of exons are kept in mature mRNA, so one gene can give several proteins.

items.stem: In which direction do ribosomes move along mRNA, and how is the polypeptide extended?
choices: 3′→5′, with each new amino acid added at the E site
5′→3′, with each new amino acid added to the free amino (N) end
3′→5′, starting at the stop codon
5′→3′, with each new amino acid added to the growing chain at the A site
items.note: The ribosome reads 5′→3′. The chain on tRNA in the P site is transferred to the amino acid in the A site.

items.stem: Insulin is made as a longer precursor that is cut to form the active hormone. This is an example of:
choices: Alternative splicing of mRNA
Removal of introns before translation
Post-translational modification
A frameshift mutation in the gene
items.note: Pre-proinsulin is cleaved after translation (signal sequence, then C-peptide removed) to give active insulin.

markscheme: RNA polymerase binds to the DNA (at the promoter) (1)
DNA strands are separated by breaking hydrogen bonds (1)
Free RNA nucleotides pair with complementary bases on the template strand (A–U, C–G) (1)
RNA polymerase joins nucleotides into a strand 5′→3′ (1)
mRNA detaches and the DNA re-forms its double helix (1)
items.tactic: Outline: key steps in order with the enzyme named.

items.stem: Explain how a single base substitution can cause sickle cell anaemia.
markscheme: GAG → GTG in the gene for the β-globin chain (1)
Codon changes so valine replaces glutamic acid (1)
Haemoglobin is less soluble at low O₂ / forms fibres, causing sickle-shaped red blood cells (1)
items.tactic: Mutation questions: DNA change → mRNA codon → amino acid → protein → phenotype.

items.stem: Describe how mRNA is processed in eukaryotic cells before translation.
markscheme: A cap is added to the 5′ end (1)
A poly-A tail is added to the 3′ end (1)
Alternative splicing can give different mRNAs from one gene (1)
items.tactic: Processing: list each modification and where on the molecule it happens.

items.stem:
(Invented data for practice.) Researchers made an invented antibiotic and tested its effect on protein production by bacteria. Protein made (arbitrary units): no antibiotic 100; antibiotic 1 µg cm⁻³ 62; 2 µg cm⁻³ 35; 5 µg cm⁻³ 12. mRNA levels were the same in all samples.
(a) Calculate the percentage decrease in protein at 2 µg cm⁻³. (b) Deduce which stage of protein synthesis is affected, with a reason. (c) Suggest why such an antibiotic would not harm human cells.
markscheme: mRNA levels unchanged, so transcription is not affected but protein is reduced (1)
(c) Bacteria have 70S ribosomes; human cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S, so the drug can target bacterial ribosomes only (1)
items.tactic: Unfamiliar context: find the syllabus idea being tested, quote the data (with units) when you describe a trend, then explain it with that idea. One marking point per linked step.
